Uber says it will roll out live video nationwide over the coming weeks. Keep in mind that availability also depends on whether the driver has live video enabled.
What happens to the video after an Uber ride?

This is the privacy detail parents should know before using the feature. Uber says the live video is encrypted. After the trip, the driver cannot access the recording. The teen cannot access it either. The linked parent or guardian also loses access once the ride ends.

However, the encrypted recording does remain on Uber's servers for a period of time. Uber told CyberGuy that the encrypted video recording is automatically deleted after 14 days, unless it has been shared as part of a safety report. The company says it may access the decryption key when investigating a reported safety incident. Uber says that access is limited to that safety investigation.

If a submitted file becomes part of a safety-related report, Uber says it will keep the file according to its data retention policies. So, parents get a live view during the ride, but they cannot go back later and replay the trip.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
Parents can watch their teen’s Uber ride through the driver’s front-facing smartphone camera when live video is enabled. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Why Uber is adding live video to Teen Accounts

Uber says Teen Accounts grew from an idea from parents and feedback from drivers. Since launching in 2023, the service has expanded to more than 50 countries. Uber says families now use Teen Accounts for tens of millions of trips every year.
Live video builds on safety tools already available for teen rides. Parents can use live trip tracking and PIN verification. Uber also offers audio recording as another safety feature.

The new video option gives parents something a map cannot provide: a real-time look inside the vehicle. For a parent watching a ride take an unexpected turn or run longer than expected, that extra visibility could be reassuring.
The privacy trade-off parents should know

I can see why this feature will appeal to many families. Watching your teen safely travel across town can offer reassurance that a moving dot on a map cannot provide. At the same time, you are introducing a camera feed into the ride. Parents should understand what happens to that video before deciding how often they want to use it.

Uber says only the linked parent or guardian can watch the stream live. The company also says it cannot access the live feed in real time. However, an encrypted recording can remain on Uber's servers for up to 14 days. Uber says it may access the decryption key when investigating a reported safety incident. That setup gives families more visibility during the ride while leaving an encrypted copy with Uber for a limited period afterward.
Tips for parents using Uber Teen Accounts
Live video can be helpful, but a few simple habits can make teen rides safer from the start.

Check the ride details before your teen gets in. Make sure the driver's name, vehicle and license plate match what appears in the Uber app.Talk about when you will use live video. Setting expectations ahead of time can help your teen understand whether you plan to check every ride or only when something seems unusual.Keep Uber's available safety features turned on. Use live trip tracking and PIN verification alongside live video when those tools are available for the ride.Have a backup plan. Make sure your teen knows how to contact you, reach Uber's safety tools or call 911 if they ever feel threatened or unsafe.
Check the ride details before your teen gets in. Make sure the driver's name, vehicle and license plate match what appears in the Uber app.
Talk about when you will use live video. Setting expectations ahead of time can help your teen understand whether you plan to check every ride or only when something seems unusual.
Keep Uber's available safety features turned on. Use live trip tracking and PIN verification alongside live video when those tools are available for the ride.
Have a backup plan. Make sure your teen knows how to contact you, reach Uber's safety tools or call 911 if they ever feel threatened or unsafe.
It is also worth reminding your teen to trust their instincts. If the driver, vehicle or situation looks different from what appears in the app, they should stay out of the car and contact you.
What this means to you

If your teenager already uses Uber, live video gives you another way to check on a ride without repeatedly calling or texting. Still, I would talk with your teen before the feature becomes part of your routine.

Some parents may want to open the feed only when something seems off. Others may check briefly at the beginning of a ride. The right approach will depend on your teen's age and how much independence your family is comfortable giving them.

Also, remember that live video depends on the driver having the feature enabled. You should still pay attention to the trip details shown in the Uber app. Technology can give you more visibility, but your teen should also know what to do when a ride feels wrong.
RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS
Uber’s new Teen Accounts feature alerts both the teen and driver when a linked parent begins watching the live video. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I like that Uber is giving parents more visibility into teen rides and alerting both the driver and teen when a parent starts watching. That transparency makes sense when a camera enters the ride. Still, parents should understand the full privacy picture. The live feed ends for the family when the trip ends, while an encrypted recording can remain on Uber's servers for up to 14 days. Uber says it may decrypt that recording when investigating a reported safety incident. For me, live video works best as a tool you can reach for when you need reassurance rather than something you feel compelled to watch for an entire ride. Teens need opportunities to build independence. Parents also need practical ways to respond when something feels wrong.

title: What a smart firewall does and why it matters on home Wi-Fi
summary: Router firewalls and software firewalls serve different roles in protecting your home Wi-Fi from unwanted traffic and suspicious connections.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson warned of worrying privacy clauses in smart devices in a recent episode of the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Most of us think of home Wi-Fi as the invisible connection that lets a laptop stream a movie, a phone display photos and a printer work from across the room. In practice, it is also the meeting point for many devices, accounts and types of information. A typical home network may include computers, phones, tablets, smart speakers, televisions, cameras, printers and connected appliances. These devices regularly send and receive data.

Some of that traffic is expected, such as opening a bank website or downloading a software update. Other traffic may be unwanted or suspicious. That is where a firewall comes in. A firewall is a security system that checks network connections and applies rules about which traffic should be allowed. Think of it as a doorman for digital connections. It does not know everything about every visitor, but it can help prevent some unexpected traffic from reaching a device.
Understanding how firewalls work, where they fit and what they can and cannot protect against can help you make smarter choices about securing your home Wi-Fi.

FBI SAYS RUSSIAN HACKERS HIJACKED OLD WI-FI ROUTERS

A firewall can help protect home Wi-Fi by controlling network connections, but it works best alongside updated software, strong passwords and backups. (Gavin Roberts/MacFormat Magazine/Future via Getty Images)
Router firewall vs software firewall

Your router is the box that connects your home to the internet and sends Wi-Fi throughout the house. Many home routers include a built-in firewall. Because it sits at the gateway, this router firewall can help protect devices connected to your home network from certain unwanted connections coming from the internet.

A router firewall is useful because one device can provide a basic layer of protection for the network as a whole. It can help reduce direct exposure for computers, phones and other connected equipment. However, its settings and capabilities depend on the router model, its software and how it was configured.

A software firewall runs on an individual device, such as a Windows PC or Mac. It can add another layer of awareness and control at the device level. This becomes especially useful when a laptop leaves home, connects to a different network or needs to distinguish between applications running on that computer.
TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK

The two types can work together. A router firewall and a software firewall serve different purposes. The router helps guard the network's front door, while the software firewall helps watch activity involving a particular device.
What inbound and outbound traffic mean
The terms sound technical, but the basic idea is straightforward.

Inbound traffic is data traveling toward your device. For example, a website may send information back to your browser after you request a page, or a remote computer may try to connect to a service on your network. Some inbound traffic is expected, especially when it responds to a connection you started. Other inbound traffic may be unexpected.

Outbound traffic is data leaving your device. Opening a webpage, sending an email, uploading a photograph or syncing a file all involve outbound activity. If an unfamiliar program tries to connect to the internet, that may also be outbound traffic.
CHEAP STREAMING BOX COULD HIJACK YOUR HOME INTERNET

A firewall may use rules, application information and other signals to decide whether a connection looks familiar or requires attention. Depending on the operating system and security product, it may alert you, allow the connection or block it. The goal is to help ordinary online activity continue while making unusual network behavior more visible and manageable.
Why network awareness deserves more attention now

Online banking and shopping place sensitive information at the center of ordinary internet use. You may sign in to a bank, enter a card number, review a medical bill or manage a retirement account from the same computer you use for entertainment.
BEWARE OF HACKERS SHOWING UP PRETENDING TO BE IT

Remote work adds another reason to pay attention. A home laptop may handle work documents, personal files and video meetings throughout the day. If an unfamiliar application begins communicating online, security tools that provide additional context can help you understand what the computer is doing.

A firewall cannot tell whether every website, email or message is honest. A scammer may persuade someone to visit a legitimate-looking page or approve an action that appears convincing. A firewall provides one layer of protection, while your decisions remain an important part of staying safe.
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES
What a firewall can and cannot do

A firewall can help control certain network connections. It may reduce exposure to some unsolicited inbound traffic and help identify unusual activity involving applications. It can also add a layer of protection when a device connects to networks outside the home.

A firewall cannot make a weak password strong or determine whether someone is being tricked by a convincing text message. It also cannot replace antivirus protection, software updates, multifactor authentication, secure router settings or reliable backups.

No firewall can guarantee that files, accounts or devices will never be compromised. Some threats arrive through activity you intentionally start, such as opening a malicious attachment or entering information into a fake website. Other threats may exploit weaknesses in outdated software. Those situations call for additional defenses and safer habits.
HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS
Router and software firewalls provide different layers of protection by monitoring connections at the network and individual device levels. (Fabian Sommer/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Home Wi-Fi basics worth checking
A few simple router and Wi-Fi settings can strengthen your home network and reduce unnecessary security risks.

Start with the router. Use the security mode recommended by the manufacturer or internet provider and avoid leaving the administrator password at its default. The administrator password controls important router settings and should be different from the Wi-Fi password.
Install router firmware updates when they are offered. Firmware is the built-in software that helps the router operate. Updates may improve performance, fix problems or address security weaknesses.
Use a strong, unique Wi-Fi password. If your router offers a guest network, consider using it for visitors or devices that do not need access to your main network.
Review the list of connected devices occasionally so you know what is using your Wi-Fi. If you see a device you do not recognize, investigate it and change your Wi-Fi password if needed.

Consider replacing a router that no longer receives security updates or cannot support current security standards. Check the manufacturer's documentation rather than assuming that a newer Wi-Fi label automatically gives you stronger security.
A firewall provides one layer of protection
A firewall works best as part of a broader security setup that protects your devices, accounts and important files.
Keep your operating system, browser, apps and router updated. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available.
Use multifactor authentication for banking, email and other important accounts. Multifactor authentication adds a second verification step, such as an approval on your phone, after your password.

Be cautious with unexpected links, attachments and urgent requests for payment or personal information. Scammers often rely on urgency to get you to act before you have time to question what is happening.
Before approving a remote-access request, confirm who is asking and why. If an alert appears, read it carefully rather than automatically allowing or dismissing it.

Firewalls, antivirus software and backups each protect you in a different way. A firewall helps control network connections, antivirus software detects and responds to malicious software, and reliable backups can help you recover important files if they are damaged, deleted or locked by ransomware. Together, these protections create a stronger defense than any one tool can provide alone.

When choosing antivirus protection, look for real-time malware and ransomware detection, phishing protection, automatic security updates and coverage for all the devices you use. Some products also include device-level firewall protection or cloud backup, but features, storage limits and compatibility can vary by platform.
Visit CyberGuy’s best antivirus protection guide for our current recommendations, comparisons and special offers for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Protecting the files you cannot replace

Your computer may hold years of family photos, tax returns, medical records, scanned IDs, insurance documents and other files that would be difficult or impossible to replace. That makes protecting your data just as important as protecting the computer itself.

Ransomware is malicious software that can lock or encrypt your files and then demand payment to restore access. A firewall may help block or limit some suspicious connections, but ransomware can reach a device in other ways. Strong security habits and reliable backups give you a better chance of recovering if something goes wrong.

A useful guideline is the 3-2-1 backup strategy: keep three copies of important data on two different types of storage, with at least one copy stored separately from your computer. CISA guidance recommends this approach as one way to improve your ability to recover from ransomware.

Backups work best when they are automatic, current and separated from the same incident affecting your computer. Test a few backed-up files occasionally to make sure you can open them. When practical, keep at least one backup disconnected from your computer or otherwise isolated from routine activity. CISA recommends offline backups because some ransomware can also reach connected storage. Protect cloud backup accounts with strong, unique passwords and multifactor authentication. Norton AntiVirus Plus includes 2 GB of PC Cloud Backup on eligible Windows systems.

If your files suddenly become encrypted, disconnect the affected computer from the network if you can do so safely. CISA recommends isolating affected systems, including disconnecting them from Wi-Fi when necessary, to help prevent the infection from spreading. Avoid rushing to pay a ransom or deleting potential evidence. Preserve messages and notes about what happened and check whether clean backups are available. Consider contacting a qualified cybersecurity professional for help. If you believe an account may also have been exposed, change important passwords from a separate, trusted device.
FCC ROUTER RULE RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT FUTURE UPDATES
Checking router settings, installing firmware updates and reviewing connected devices can help strengthen home Wi-Fi security. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

A firewall does a lot of work you may never see, and that is exactly why it can be easy to overlook. Your router firewall helps protect the network at home, while a software firewall can watch connections involving a specific computer wherever you take it. I would use both when available, but I would never count on a firewall by itself. Strong passwords, multifactor authentication, current software, antivirus protection and dependable backups all cover risks that a firewall cannot handle. The bigger point is visibility. Most of us have dozens of connections happening behind the scenes every time we use a computer. A good firewall gives you another set of eyes on that activity and another opportunity to stop something suspicious before it goes further.

title: Fake Chrome update scam could infect your computer
summary: A Chrome extension with 70,000 users and a 4.7-star rating began injecting fake update warnings after a threat actor acquired and weaponized it.
story: Smart refrigerators, cars and computers can show ads after updates, raising privacy and ownership concerns, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You are browsing the web when a warning suddenly takes over the page. It says your browser needs a "Critical Update" before you can continue. It looks like Chrome. The message feels urgent. So, clicking Update may seem like the safest thing you can do. That is exactly what makes this fake Chrome update scam so convincing.

Recent reports linked aggressive fake browser update warnings to a Chrome extension called Enable Right Click & Copy - Smart Unlock + OCR. The extension was originally developed as a legitimate tool for restoring right-click and copying features on websites that block them. However, security researchers at Socket now say the extension was later acquired by a threat actor and updated with malicious functionality. It had around 70,000 users when that malicious functionality appeared, although researchers caution that this does not mean every user received the malicious version. The extension was delisted from the Chrome Web Store on Aug. 14 after being flagged as potentially malicious.
FAKE WINDOWS UPDATE INSTALLS HIDDEN MALWARE
Fake Google Chrome update prompts may appear on normal websites and urge users to download unfamiliar files instead of updating through Chrome itself. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The bigger lesson goes beyond one extension. Something you installed months ago and trusted every day can change after an update. Here's how this fake Chrome update scam works, how to spot the warning signs and what you can do to protect your browser and computer.

How the fake Chrome update scam works

The warning can appear while you are visiting an otherwise normal website. You may see language such as "Critical Update Required" or "Update available." The alert then pushes you to download something before you continue browsing.

However, Chrome normally handles its updates through the browser itself. Google says Chrome usually updates automatically in the background. You can also check manually by opening Chrome and going to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

A webpage asking you to download a .vbs script or an unfamiliar .exe file to update Chrome should immediately raise your suspicion. Google specifically advises users to avoid suspicious pop-ups asking them to install updates. Instead, Google recommends going directly to the program or its official website.
Why a trusted extension can suddenly become dangerous

Here is the part that can catch careful people off guard. You may have installed an extension when it had thousands of users, strong reviews and no obvious signs of trouble. You use it for months. Then the extension changes.

Google confirmed to CyberGuy that it looked into Enable Right Click & Copy - Smart Unlock + OCR. "We've investigated the extension and taken action to protect our users," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

New research published by Socket on Aug. 27 shows the threat went beyond fake update warnings. Researchers linked the extension to a larger campaign involving 19 Chrome and Edge extensions capable of delivering malicious payloads. Those capabilities included credential theft, cryptocurrency wallet draining, injected phishing pages and fake browser update lures. Socket says some of the extensions began as legitimate products before being acquired and weaponized by the threat actor.

We have seen that pattern before. Earlier this year, researchers found that QuickLens - Search Screen with Google Lens changed ownership before a malicious update arrived. The extension had previously earned a Featured badge from Google. Researchers later found malicious functionality capable of injecting code, displaying fake Google update prompts and targeting sensitive information. Google removed QuickLens from the Chrome Web Store.

CyberGuy has also reported on trusted browser extensions that later became spyware. One campaign affected 4.3 million users after extensions that began as useful tools eventually received malicious updates. That history changes how I look at browser extensions. A great rating tells you what people thought when they reviewed an extension. It cannot guarantee what a future update will do.
Why the 4.7-star rating should get your attention

This recent extension case had another detail I think everyone should notice. Enable Right Click & Copy - Smart Unlock + OCR still had an average rating near 4.7 stars as reports of the fake update warnings appeared. That can happen because thousands of earlier positive ratings remain part of the overall score.

Meanwhile, recent reviews can begin filling with warnings. In this case, August reviews accused the extension of injecting fake Chrome update alerts. Several users said removing or disabling it stopped the prompts.

So, before installing an extension, look beyond the overall star rating. Read the newest reviews as well. CyberGuy previously covered another browser-extension scam involving a fake ad blocker. That extension created computer problems and then tried to convince users to run dangerous commands to fix them.
Why antivirus software may not immediately explain the problem
One Reddit user who encountered the recent fake update warnings said a full scan found nothing. The user later traced the pop-ups to the Right Click extension.

A clean scan should never convince you that a suspicious browser warning is safe. The extension itself may be creating or injecting what you see inside the browser. Meanwhile, a downloaded malicious file may pose a separate threat if you open or execute it.

Google's Safe Browsing system checks installed extensions and downloads against known threats. Chrome can also disable extensions that Google identifies as malicious. Still, newly emerging threats can create a window where users encounter trouble before defenses catch up. That is why your own reaction to a suspicious prompt remains important.
FAKE CAPTCHA SCAM CAN HACK YOUR COMPUTER
A fake Chrome update scam linked to a once-legitimate browser extension can push users to download dangerous files disguised as critical updates. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
This can happen outside Google Chrome
Seeing a Chrome-branded warning inside another browser gives you a pretty good clue that something is wrong.

Users of Chromium-based browsers including Brave and Opera have reported similar fake Chrome update prompts. Users connected those warnings with suspicious browser extensions rather than genuine browser updates.

That makes sense because Chromium-based browsers can support many of the same types of browser extensions. If Opera suddenly tells you that Google Chrome desperately needs an update, do not follow the prompt.
How to check whether Chrome really needs an update
You never need to trust a random webpage to tell you whether Chrome needs updating. On your computer:
Open Chrome > click the three-dot menu > Help > About Google Chrome.

Chrome will check for available updates on that page. If an update has already been downloaded, you may see an option to relaunch Chrome. If you do not see Relaunch, Google says you are running the latest available version. That simple check can take much of the guesswork out of a scary update warning.
How to remove a suspicious Chrome extension

Look carefully at what you have installed. Google lets you turn an extension off temporarily or remove it completely. You can also open an extension's details and review whether it can read or change data on every website you visit.

If you have Enable Right Click & Copy - Smart Unlock + OCR installed, I would remove it even if you never clicked or opened one of the suspicious downloads. Researchers found malicious capabilities that went beyond the fake update prompts. Then restart Chrome, run a full security scan and change passwords for sensitive accounts you used while the extension was installed from another trusted device.

If you have several unfamiliar extensions, disable them and re-enable only the ones you recognize and still need. For more help identifying warning signs, CyberGuy has a full guide explaining how to tell if your browser has been hijacked.
How to stay safe from fake Chrome update scams
A few smart habits can lower your chances of turning a convincing pop-up into a serious security problem.

If a webpage tells you to download an update, close the warning. Then go directly to Chrome > Help > About Google Chrome. Google also warns people to use caution when websites claim you need to download software because your device has a virus.

Strong antivirus protection adds another defense between a bad download and your computer. Look for antivirus software that provides real-time protection, rather than relying only on occasional manual scans. Real-time protection can monitor files as they arrive and look for suspicious behavior before malware gets a chance to spread.

Keep the antivirus software updated as well. New threats appear constantly, so outdated security software can leave gaps. If you clicked a fake update or accidentally ran a suspicious file, perform a full system scan. Follow the antivirus program's instructions if it detects malware. Pay particular attention to extensions that can read and change your data on all websites you visit. Google classifies access to data across all websites as a higher-risk permission because an extension may be able to read, request or modify information on pages you visit. If an extension suddenly asks for broader permissions or you no longer remember why you installed it, I would remove it.
FAKE PARTY INVITATION SCAM CAN HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
Browser extensions can become dangerous after ownership changes or malicious updates, even if they once had strong ratings and thousands of users. (Serene Lee/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images)

Do not rely only on the overall rating. Scroll down and look at what people have written recently. A long history of five-star reviews can hide a sudden change that users discovered only days ago. If recent reviews suddenly mention pop-ups, malware or unexpected redirects, choose another extension.

For additional protection, open: Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Security > Enhanced protection. Google says Enhanced Protection can warn you about potentially dangerous websites, downloads and extensions, including threats that Chrome has not previously identified. It also provides deeper checks on suspicious downloads.

If you clicked a fake update and it downloaded a .vbs, .exe or another unfamiliar file, do not open it. Delete it. Then empty your Recycle Bin or Trash and run a full security scan. Chrome may also block files it considers dangerous, suspicious or unverified. Treat those warnings seriously rather than overriding them to get the download through.

A data removal service cannot remove malware from your computer. However, it can reduce another piece of the scammer's advantage: the amount of personal information about you that sits online. Data brokers can collect details such as contact information, previous addresses and other identifying information. Scammers can use exposed data to make follow-up phishing attempts feel much more believable. For example, a scammer who already knows your name, phone number and where you live has more material to personalize a fake security alert. Data removal services work by sending removal requests to data brokers and other sites that publish personal information. They can also continue checking whether your information reappears. Reducing that digital footprint will never stop every scam. However, giving criminals less information to work with can make targeted attacks harder to personalize. If you actually executed the suspicious file, treat the computer as potentially compromised.

What to do if the fake Chrome update keeps appearing
If you removed a suspicious extension and the warning still appears, continue narrowing down the cause.

Kurt's key takeaways

What bothers me most about this fake Chrome update scam is how little suspicious behavior it requires from the person being targeted. You could have downloaded a useful extension from the official Chrome Web Store. It could have worked exactly as promised. It could even have thousands of happy users. Then something changes behind the scenes. That means we need to stop treating browser extensions as install-once-and-forget-about-it utilities. Every extension gets a level of access to your browser. The fewer you keep around, the smaller that exposure becomes. I would also make one rule nonnegotiable: Never update Chrome because a webpage tells you to download a file. title: Amazon makes Alexa+ free on compatible Fire TVs
summary: Amazon's Alexa+ rolls out free to Fire TV devices across the U.S., but hands-free microphones and stored voice data raise key privacy questions.
story: Daniel Rausch, Amazon Alexa & Echo VP, highlights the transformative AI overhaul of Alexa, now called Alexa+. He reveals how the new system, including "Alexa for Shopping", boosts customer engagement three-fold by automating deal alerts and managing daily tasks.

AI is coming to your TV, and if you own a compatible Fire TV, Amazon may add it without you doing anything. Amazon is rolling out Alexa+ to compatible Fire TV devices across the U.S. at no additional cost. You do not need an Amazon Prime membership for the Fire TV experience. There is no app to download or subscription to activate either. Eligible devices get upgraded automatically.
That means millions of televisions and streaming devices are gaining a more conversational AI assistant. But what you probably really want to know is: What can you actually say to it?

There is also a privacy question worth answering. Some Fire TV devices have hands-free microphones while others rely on the microphone button on the remote. Alexa also stores information about your interactions depending on your settings. So, here is how to try Alexa+ on your Fire TV and how to check the controls behind it.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. ALEXA+ LETS YOU ORDER FOOD LIKE A REAL CONVERSATION
Amazon is rolling out Alexa+ at no additional cost to compatible Fire TV devices in the U.S., giving users more conversational voice search and smart home controls. (Amazon)
What Alexa+ changes on your Fire TV
The old Alexa worked best when you gave it a fairly direct command. Alexa+ can understand more natural conversations and follow-up questions.
For example, you can describe the kind of movie you want rather than knowing its title. Then you can narrow the results without repeating your entire request.

Amazon says Alexa+ users are having nearly twice as many conversations on Fire TV compared with the original Alexa. The company also says viewers choose Alexa's top movie recommendation more than 40% more often than they did previously.
The assistant reaches beyond entertainment too. It can interact with compatible smart home devices and display supported camera feeds. You can also ask general questions while you watch TV.
How to start using Alexa+ on Fire TV
How you talk to Alexa+ depends on the Fire TV hardware you have.

If you use a Fire TV Stick: Press and hold the Alexa or microphone button on your Alexa Voice Remote. Say what you want, then release the button. Amazon says current Fire TV Sticks use the remote for voice control. Hands-free control requires a linked Echo device.

If you use a Fire TV Cube: You can press the microphone button on the remote or speak to Alexa from across the room. The current Fire TV Cube supports native hands-free Alexa through its built-in microphone array.

If Alexa is built into your smart TV: Capabilities vary by model. Some supported televisions have hands-free Alexa while others rely on the voice remote or a linked Echo. Amazon's device specifications identify which models support far-field voice control.
Once Alexa+ appears on your Fire TV, there is no special Alexa+ mode you need to open. Just start talking to it.
Try these Alexa+ commands on your Fire TV

The real fun starts when you stop treating Alexa like a search box. Try conversational requests and follow up naturally. Some features depend on the streaming service, your subscriptions and the smart home devices connected to Alexa.

Finding something to watch: "Alexa, find a highly rated thriller from the last five years."Narrowing the results: "Make it something funny instead."Finding family entertainment: "Show me family movies that are under two hours."Learning about what you are watching: "Alexa, who is this actor and what else have they been in?"Moving between TVs: "Alexa, move this show to the bedroom Fire TV."Finding a movie moment: "Alexa, jump to the restaurant scene in this movie." Amazon says scene jumping works with thousands of supported Prime Video movies.Checking your front door: "Alexa, show me the front-door camera."Changing the room: "Alexa, dim the living-room lights for movie night."Checking sports: "Alexa, what's the score of the Yankees game?"Doing something without grabbing your phone: "Alexa, set a 20-minute timer."

Amazon specifically highlights conversational entertainment searches, follow-up questions, Ring camera feeds, smart home controls and general information requests as part of Alexa+ on Fire TV. It also supports jumping directly to described scenes in thousands of Prime Video movies.
That last feature may be especially useful when you are trying to find one memorable moment without dragging the progress bar back and forth.
CHEAP STREAMING BOX COULD HIJACK YOUR HOME INTERNET

Alexa+ lets compatible Fire TV owners search for movies using natural language, ask follow-up questions and control supported smart home devices. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Amazon products that work well with the new Alexa+ experience
If your current television still works perfectly, a streaming stick may be the easiest way to add the newer Fire TV experience.

Amazon's latest Fire TV Stick HD supports Wi-Fi 6 and includes voice control through the Fire TV remote. It is designed for HD streaming and can also work with a linked Echo for hands-free Alexa control.
The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus supports 4K Ultra HD, Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and Dolby Atmos. It includes an Alexa Voice Remote. Like the other current sticks, hands-free Alexa requires a linked Echo.

The Fire TV Cube makes the most sense if you specifically want to speak to Alexa without reaching for the remote. Amazon's current Cube has a four-microphone array and supports native hands-free Alexa.
To compare these Fire TV options and find links to the models we recommend, visit CyberGuy.com.
Is your Fire TV microphone always listening?

This is where the type of Fire TV you own makes a big difference. If you have a Fire TV Stick, the streaming stick itself does not provide native hands-free Alexa. You normally press the microphone button on the Alexa Voice Remote when you want to speak. Amazon says a blue indicator appears on the television when the remote is recording your request and sending it to the cloud. If you pair that Fire TV Stick with an Echo, the Echo can provide hands-free voice control.

The Fire TV Cube works differently. It has built-in microphones designed to hear the Alexa wake word from across the room. Amazon says supported hands-free Fire TV devices use on-device wake-word detection. Once the device recognizes the wake word, audio is sent to Amazon's cloud for processing. Amazon says that audio can include a fraction of a second from immediately before the wake word. That is worth knowing before you start using Alexa+ heavily.
How to physically turn off a hands-free Fire TV microphone

If your Fire TV device supports hands-free Alexa, look for its microphone-off button or switch. Amazon says using that control disconnects power to the microphones. A red light appears to show that the microphones are disabled.

With the microphones off, that device cannot record or stream audio when you say the Alexa wake word. You can still use an Alexa Voice Remote because the remote has its own microphone that activates when you press its voice button. That gives you a useful middle ground. You can disable hands-free listening while keeping voice commands available whenever you intentionally press the remote button.
Turn off Alexa Follow Up Mode if you want less listening

Alexa can support follow-up requests so you do not have to repeat the wake word every time. If you prefer Alexa to stop listening after each request, Amazon says you can disable Follow Up Mode in your device settings or through the Alexa app. There is an even easier option. Say: "Alexa, turn off Follow Up Mode." Amazon confirms that voice command can disable the feature.
Check what Alexa has saved about you
If you are going to use Alexa+ more often, I would spend a minute looking at your Alexa history.
Open the Alexa app > More > Alexa Privacy > Review Alexa History.
Open the Alexa app > More > Alexa Privacy > Review Alexa History.
Here you can review voice recordings, transcripts and typed Alexa requests associated with your Amazon account. Amazon says you can also delete them.
Next, go to Alexa app > More > Alexa Privacy > Manage Your Alexa Data.
Next, go to Alexa app > More > Alexa Privacy > Manage Your Alexa Data.
Amazon provides controls here for managing how your voice recordings are retained and whether they can be used to improve its services.
If you use Alexa to control lights, cameras or other connected equipment, check More > Alexa Privacy > Manage Your Alexa Data > Smart Home Device History as well.

Amazon says you can delete that history or have certain smart home information automatically deleted after three or 18 months. Keep in mind that deleting Alexa history may affect personalization and certain Alexa features.
NEW AMAZON AI SEARCH TURNS WORDS INTO SHOPPABLE IMAGES
Fire TV Stick users activate Alexa+ through the voice remote, while compatible Fire TV Cube models support hands-free Alexa through built-in microphones. (Amazon)
Check these privacy controls directly on Fire TV too
Alexa privacy is only one part of the equation. Fire TV has its own data settings.

Amazon's current instructions point to Settings > Preferences > Privacy Settings on Fire TV products.Look for Device Usage Data. Turning this off tells Amazon to stop processing that device-usage information for customized marketing offers and product improvement.Then check Collect App Usage Data. This controls Amazon's collection of information about when you open and close third-party apps and how long you use them.You can also review Interest-based Ads if you want to reduce personalized advertising.
Amazon's current instructions point to Settings > Preferences > Privacy Settings on Fire TV products.
Look for Device Usage Data. Turning this off tells Amazon to stop processing that device-usage information for customized marketing offers and product improvement.
Then check Collect App Usage Data. This controls Amazon's collection of information about when you open and close third-party apps and how long you use them.
You can also review Interest-based Ads if you want to reduce personalized advertising.

Amazon notes that turning these settings off does not stop every form of data collection. Some device information still gets processed to provide features, troubleshoot problems and operate Amazon services. Apps such as Prime Video may have separate privacy controls too. These settings are device-specific. If you have more than one Fire TV in the house, Amazon says you need to review the settings on each one.
What Alexa+ costs now

Here is an important detail that could easily get lost in the word "free." Compatible Fire TV owners in the U.S. can now use many Alexa+ features on their television at no additional charge, regardless of whether they have Prime.

However, Amazon still charges $19.99 a month for its broader Alexa+ Standard Plan for non-Prime members. Prime members receive the broader Alexa+ experience as part of Prime. Prime or the Alexa+ Standard Plan also unlocks additional capabilities. Amazon lists Alexa Routines, access to specific Ring camera moments and advanced Home Modes among the extra Fire TV features. Subscribers also get Alexa+ on compatible Echo devices. So, you can get plenty of Alexa+ functionality on a compatible Fire TV without paying another monthly fee. Just do not assume every Alexa+ feature across every Amazon device has become free.
What this means to you

For most Fire TV owners, the biggest improvement will probably be search. Scrolling through endless rows of movies can get old fast. Being able to describe what you want and then refine the results by talking naturally could make Alexa+ genuinely useful. Smart home controls add another layer. If you already use Ring cameras, compatible lights or connected locks, the television becomes another place to manage them. The automatic upgrade deserves attention too.

You may suddenly have an AI assistant with new capabilities on a device you have owned for years. That makes this a good time to understand whether your particular Fire TV has hands-free microphones and review the privacy choices connected to Alexa. You can use the convenience without leaving every data setting untouched.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like the direction Amazon is taking with Alexa+ on Fire TV because voice search badly needed an upgrade. Asking for a movie the way you would describe it to a friend feels far more useful than remembering an exact title. The hands-on features are where this gets interesting. I can see myself asking about an actor while watching a movie or pulling up a front-door camera without reaching for my phone. Still, an automatic AI upgrade should also trigger an automatic privacy check in your head. First, find out where the microphone actually lives. A Fire TV Stick's remote works differently from the hands-free microphones in a Fire TV Cube. Then look through Alexa Privacy and the Fire TV Privacy Settings menu. You may decide you are comfortable with everything exactly as Amazon configured it. You may also find a few switches you would rather change. Either way, that choice should belong to you.
Would you rather have Alexa+ automatically added to your Fire TV, or should Amazon make AI features like this something you choose to turn on yourself? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: What Meta's new teen restrictions mean for young people
summary: Meta's new teen accounts settlement sets a default two-hour daily limit on Instagram and Facebook, plus night mode and school mode restrictions.
story: Tech policy expert Clare Morell joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze the impact of Meta's youth addiction settlement, which mandates a two-hour daily limit for Facebook and Instagram users under 18. The historic agreement blocks apps from midnight to 6 a.m. and silences school-hour notifications.
If you have ever asked a teenager to put down a phone and heard, "Just one more minute," you already know how hard screen limits can be to enforce.
Now Meta has agreed to a sweeping child-safety settlement that could reshape how teens use Facebook and Instagram across much of the United States.

A judge approved the agreement on Aug. 27. Under the deal, Meta will put a default two-hour daily cap on teen use of Facebook and Instagram combined. It will also restrict most app access overnight. Meanwhile, parents will get stronger control over settings teens may want to change.
The agreement goes well beyond a screen time reminder. Here's what will change, how the limits work, what Meta told CyberGuy and what parents can do now.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS
Meta says teen accounts will continue using age-appropriate content settings while the company strengthens protections for younger users. (Meta)
How Meta's new restrictions could change a teen's day

With the judge's approval, the agreement is now in effect, but the new protections will roll out over the coming months. Most of the major requirements have a six-month compliance deadline, while some features are due sooner. Here's how the biggest changes break down for teens and parents.

Meta will apply a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram combined. Time spent scrolling on either app counts toward the total. In addition, Meta says it will count usage across multiple accounts when it detects that one teen operates more than one account.

Direct messaging, time spent in settings and qualifying long-form audio or video are excluded from the two-hour limit. Under the agreement, qualifying long-form content generally means audio or video that lasts at least 22 minutes and has not been artificially extended.
A teen can only turn off the two-hour limit with a parent's permission. That creates a much firmer stopping point than another reminder that can be dismissed.
Meta already offers parental time-management tools on Instagram, while the proposed settlement would add a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram. (Meta)
Night Mode will block most Facebook and Instagram activity from midnight to 6 a.m. During that window, teens will no longer be able to view or post to areas such as Feed, Stories, Explore or Reels.

Direct messaging will remain available. That exception lets teens continue communicating with friends and family. For families dealing with late-night scrolling, this could create a clearer boundary without requiring someone to change the setting every evening.
Meta will also disable push notifications by default from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., except for urgent account security or platform integrity alerts. Parents using supervision can change that setting.
School Mode focuses on daytime distractions. From 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday between Aug. 15 and June 15, Meta will mute most push notifications by default.

However, teens will still be able to receive direct messages. Meta will also allow account security and safety alerts during those hours. The idea is simple. A school day should come with fewer reasons to keep checking Instagram or Facebook.

Meta will also add more frequent reminders. Teens will receive a prompt after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram. In addition, Meta will send prompts when total daily use reaches 60 minutes and again at 90 minutes.
The settlement requires these prompts and pauses to be implemented within four months of the agreement's effective date.
Those alerts arrive before a teen reaches the two-hour limit. As a result, the hard cap becomes the final boundary rather than the first warning.

The agreement also changes parts of the viewing experience. Teens will be able to choose a non-personalized feed as their default. That feed will avoid Meta's recommendation systems when deciding what to show next.

Parents using supervision will be able to require that setting. Meta will also periodically remind teens that the option exists. Meanwhile, teens will be able to turn off autoplay. Parents will be able to require that setting too. With autoplay disabled, another piece of content will no longer begin automatically. The teen will need to tap or swipe to continue.
NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN
Instagram gives teens ways to shape what they see, while the new agreement adds more controls around how young users experience Meta’s apps. (Meta)
Meta will hide like and reaction totals by default for teen accounts. That applies to a teen's own posts as well as content posted by other people.

The company is also expanding its restrictions on appearance filters. Meta already blocks teens from using cosmetic surgery filters. Under the agreement, teens will also lose access to what Meta calls extreme makeup filters. These changes target parts of the social media experience that can keep attention focused on appearance and social feedback.
Age verification sits at the center of these protections. A teen limit only works if the platform correctly identifies the person behind the account.

Meta says it will invest in stronger technology to find accounts that may belong to children under 13. The company also plans to improve systems that identify users ages 13 to 17 who enter an adult birthday. Once Meta identifies those accounts, it can place them into experiences designed for teens.
Still, age detection remains one of the biggest tests ahead. A system that regularly mistakes teens for adults could weaken many of the protections in the agreement.

Meta also plans to expand its parental supervision tools. For example, parents will receive a notification when a teen links a secondary account. The company also plans alerts involving interactions with accounts it considers potentially suspicious.

In addition, parents will get periodic updates about their teen's usage and attempts to change protective settings. Those alerts could make it easier to catch changes without constantly checking a teen's account.
Meta’s Teen Accounts include built-in privacy and safety settings, with parents able to help manage certain protections for users under 18. (Meta)
Meta's Teen Accounts already laid the groundwork

Meta began rolling out Teen Accounts in 2024. Those accounts brought automatic protections to younger Instagram users and added more control for parents. Meta later expanded its teen safety approach across more of its services.
CyberGuy previously covered Meta's expansion of Teen Accounts to Facebook and Messenger. Earlier tools leaned more heavily on reminders and configurable controls.

By comparison, the settlement creates stronger defaults. A teen who reaches the two-hour combined limit will need a parent's permission to turn it off. For a household where "five more minutes" somehow turns into another hour, that could feel very different.
Why TikTok and YouTube are tied to Meta's payout
Meta describes the financial package as approximately $18 billion. Participating states would receive about 70% of the allocated payment, or roughly $12.7 billion, over 10 years.

The remaining 30%, about $5.3 billion, depends on TikTok and YouTube meeting two conditions. First, both companies would need to implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode and age-assurance measures. Second, each would need to make a matching financial payment.

Half of Meta's remaining funds would be tied to YouTube's payment. The other half would depend on TikTok. Meta argues that restricting teens on one platform has limited impact if they can immediately move to another app. That helps explain why two of its biggest rivals play such a prominent role in the agreement.

The executed agreement also includes Snap in the broader industry-adoption framework. However, Meta's public explanation ties the matching financial-payment requirement specifically to TikTok and YouTube.
Meta is calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar teen protections, including daily time limits, overnight restrictions and stronger age checks. (Meta)
Meta calls for an industry-wide approach

Meta responded to CyberGuy with additional information about the agreement, including an open letter calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same framework. According to Meta, teens regularly move among many apps, so similar protections need to extend across the industry.

Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney made the same case in an on-camera statement provided to CyberGuy. He said, " Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution."

Mahoney also called on TikTok and YouTube to implement the framework right away. From a parent's point of view, Meta's argument is easy to understand. If Instagram closes after two hours while another social platform stays available, some teens may simply move their scrolling somewhere else.
That position also helps explain why TikTok and YouTube play such a prominent role in the settlement's financial structure.
Limits get tougher if other platforms join

Participation from Snap, TikTok and YouTube could trigger stricter Meta limits under the agreement's broader industry-adoption framework. The agreement requires most of its provisions to remain in place for 10 years. However, Meta's Time Limit and Night Mode commitments initially run for five years.
If industry peers join the agreement, those commitments extend to 10 years. The defaults would get tougher too.
Meta says the Daily Limit would drop to one hour per app. Night Mode would expand from midnight through 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. through 7 a.m.
As a result, participation from Meta's rivals could change both the length and strength of the restrictions.
Meta wants app stores involved in age checks

Meta says social media platforms should not shoulder the entire age-verification process on their own. The company argues that app stores should provide developers with verified age information. According to Meta, that could help apps apply age-appropriate protections more consistently.

Meta also supports legislation that would require app stores to verify a user's age and obtain parental approval before a teen downloads an app. That debate could become increasingly important as more platforms introduce age-based restrictions.
Independent auditors will check Meta's compliance
The agreement also creates outside oversight. An independent auditor will test Meta's compliance and report to participating states. Those reviews will happen annually for five years.

Meta says the agreement will also establish an independent social media research foundation. The company says it will provide consented user data to the foundation for research into teen well-being. That outside review could help show whether the protections work once they reach millions of accounts.
Tips to help protect your teen right now

A judge approved the settlement on Aug. 27. While the new requirements will roll out over the coming months, families can review their teen's social media settings today. Here are several places to start.

Meta's supervision tools give parents access to additional controls and account information. Once supervision is connected, parents can review available safety settings and manage certain protections. CyberGuy has steps showing you how to activate Instagram's parental supervision tools and link your teen's account. Before changing everything, talk with your teen about the settings you plan to use. Explain what you want to protect and why.

Open the phone's screen-time dashboard and look at the numbers together. You may discover that Instagram or Facebook takes up less time than expected. Another app could be responsible for a much larger share of the day. Then, use those numbers to set limits that reflect how the phone is actually being used. CyberGuy has a deeper guide to phone safety tools for parents, including screen-time controls.

Look at who can follow, message or tag your teen. Meta says it will continue using private defaults for teen Instagram accounts. Facebook will also keep restrictive default settings for teens. Meanwhile, the company plans to make it harder for potentially suspicious adults to find or interact with younger users. Also review followers your teen no longer recognizes.

Meta says teens will remain in age-appropriate content settings by default. The company also plans to continue restricting interactions with accounts it considers inappropriate for younger users. Parents using supervision should check those controls periodically.

Facebook and Instagram make up only part of a teen's digital day. Apple Screen Time and Google Family Link can add device-level limits. Those controls become especially useful when a teen moves from one social app to another. As a result, parents can create boundaries that extend beyond Meta's platforms.

Meta's Night Mode will add an overnight barrier inside Facebook and Instagram. Families can add another layer by charging phones outside bedrooms or keeping them in a shared space overnight. A simple routine can also reduce the nightly debate over when the phone goes away.
What these restrictions could mean for teens and parents
The two-hour cap will probably grab the most attention because it creates a clear stopping point. However, the bigger change may be how many of these protections will start turned on by default.
For teens, that could mean more interruptions during long scrolling sessions, fewer overnight opportunities to browse feeds and less pressure from notifications during school hours.
Parents will also gain more visibility when a teen tries to change certain settings. Meanwhile, Meta will face independent compliance reviews during part of the agreement period.

Age detection remains a key challenge. If a 15-year-old can easily convince the system that an account belongs to an adult, many of these protections become much easier to avoid. For that reason, the rollout will tell us far more than the announcement alone.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have watched social media companies add parental controls for years. One recurring problem keeps coming up: Parents have to find the controls before those tools can help. This agreement puts more protections on by default. A two-hour limit that requires parental permission to disable feels very different from another screen-time reminder. The overnight block could also give families some backup when late-night scrolling becomes a constant battle. I understand Meta's argument about TikTok and YouTube too. If one app closes the door while other major platforms remain available, a teen may simply move on to the next feed. Still, the real test comes as these protections roll out over the coming months. I want to see how accurately Meta identifies teen accounts and how difficult these limits are to bypass. Parents should view these tools as backup, not autopilot. Settings can create useful boundaries, but conversations at home still have to carry much of the load.

title: Healthcare data breach exposes 3.75M patient records
summary: The CareCloud data breach exposed Social Security numbers, banking information and medical records belonging to more than 3.75 million people.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You can be careful with your passwords and still get caught in a breach at a company you may have never heard of. That is one of the frustrating parts of the CareCloud data breach. More than 3.75 million people had personal information and medical records stolen after hackers gained access to a CareCloud cloud environment earlier this year.

CareCloud provides electronic medical record technology and other services to tens of thousands of healthcare providers across the U.S. So, even if you never created a CareCloud account, a doctor's office or another healthcare provider could have used its technology to handle your information. Now, we are getting a much clearer picture of just how much information hackers took.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

INSURANCE BREACH EXPOSES 7M DRIVER'S LICENSES
Healthcare providers rely on digital systems to store and manage sensitive patient information, making security a critical part of protecting medical records. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
CareCloud data breach affects more than 3.75 million people

The cyberattack dates back to March 2026. According to a breach notice filed with the California Attorney General, CareCloud experienced a network disruption on March 16. The company brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. CareCloud later determined that an unauthorized third party had access to one of its Amazon Web Services environments between March 10 and March 16, 2026.

The company said the attacker claimed to have taken data from databases inside that environment. CareCloud also said it found no evidence of continued unauthorized activity after March 16. Early disclosures showed hundreds of thousands of people were affected. However, that figure later climbed dramatically. CareCloud has now reported that more than 3.75 million people were affected, according to federal health regulators. The disclosure places the incident among the largest healthcare data breaches reported so far in 2026.
What hackers stole in the CareCloud data breach

Here is where this breach becomes especially concerning. The stolen information goes well beyond an email address or phone number. What was exposed varies from person to person, but the data may include:
Names and postal addressesSocial Security numbersMedical and health informationDriver's license numbers, passport information and other government-issued IDsBanking and other financial information
Names and postal addresses
Social Security numbers
Medical and health information
Driver's license numbers, passport information and other government-issued IDs
Banking and other financial information

Think about how much a criminal can learn from that combination. A Social Security number can help fuel identity theft. Banking information could put financial accounts at risk. Medical records can also give criminals deeply personal details that make phishing emails and scam calls far more convincing. Then there is another threat many people rarely think about: medical identity theft.
MEDICAL IDENTITY THEFT FOLLOWS YOU INTO THE DOCTOR'S OFFICE
Data breaches can expose far more than passwords, including Social Security numbers, financial details and deeply personal health information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why stolen medical information can follow you for years

You can change a password after a breach. Your medical history is much harder to replace. A criminal could use stolen insurance or personal information to seek medical care under someone else's identity. Fraudulent claims can also appear under a victim's health insurance.

In some cases, incorrect treatment or medical information could eventually make its way into someone's records. That creates problems that can extend beyond financial fraud. The Federal Trade Commission advises people who suspect medical identity theft to review their medical records and insurance statements. Look closely for unfamiliar treatments, providers, prescriptions or charges. We recently covered this growing problem in Medical identity theft follows you into the doctor's office.
What CareCloud says happened after the attack

CareCloud says it brought in outside cybersecurity specialists after discovering the incident. The company also reported the attack to law enforcement and secured the affected environment. According to its breach notice, investigators found no continued unauthorized access after the incident was contained.

CareCloud has also offered affected individuals complimentary identity protection services through IDX. If you received a notification letter, check it carefully for enrollment instructions and the amount of time you have to sign up.
CyberGuy reached out to CareCloud for comment, but we did not hear back before our deadline.
After a healthcare breach, watching your accounts, protecting your devices and staying alert for convincing scams can help reduce the risk of further damage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself after the CareCloud data breach

A breach involving Social Security numbers, medical records and financial information deserves your attention even if you have not noticed anything suspicious yet. Here are the steps I recommend taking.

Start with the letter or notification you received. Look for the specific types of information CareCloud says were involved in your case. Not every affected person necessarily had the same information exposed. If you were offered free identity protection or credit monitoring, review the terms and enrollment deadline. Consider signing up while the service remains available.

If your Social Security number was exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze limits access to your credit file. That can stop many criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. Federal law allows you to freeze and unfreeze your credit for free. However, a credit freeze cannot block every form of identity theft. Someone could still attempt to take over an existing account or misuse your personal information in other ways. For a deeper look at those limitations, read Why a credit freeze isn't the end of identity theft.

Keep an eye on your bank accounts, credit cards and credit reports. Look for purchases you do not recognize, unfamiliar credit inquiries or accounts you never opened. If something looks suspicious, contact the bank or financial institution directly. Use the phone number printed on your card or listed on the company's official website. Be wary of anyone who unexpectedly contacts you and claims they need personal information to investigate the CareCloud breach.

Do not limit your monitoring to your credit report. Sign in to your healthcare portals and review your records. Also look carefully at the explanation of benefits statements from your health insurer. Watch for unfamiliar doctors, procedures you never received or claims that make no sense. If something looks wrong, contact both your healthcare provider and insurer. Medical identity fraud may never trigger a traditional credit alert, which makes checking these records particularly important.

Use strong and unique passwords for important accounts, especially email, banking and healthcare services. If you reuse the same password on multiple sites, change it. A password manager can generate and securely store complex passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it is available. That extra verification step can make it harder for someone to get into an account even if they obtain your password. Pay extra attention to your primary email account. Criminals can use access to your inbox to reset passwords for other services.

A stolen medical record could give a scammer enough personal information to send you a very convincing message. You might receive an email that appears to come from a doctor, health insurer or breach-response company. The message could include a malicious attachment or direct you to a fake login page. Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious links, dangerous downloads and other threats that arrive through phishing emails or scam messages. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have strong antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, helping keep your personal information and digital assets safer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

This breach creates another problem. Scammers may now have enough real information about victims to sound believable. Be skeptical if someone suddenly contacts you claiming to represent CareCloud, your doctor, your insurance company or a credit-monitoring service. A criminal might know your name, address or other personal details. That knowledge does not make the person contacting you legitimate. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages. Instead, open the organization's official website yourself or call a number you already trust. Also be suspicious of anyone demanding immediate payment or asking you to provide a verification code.

The information stolen from CareCloud can become even more useful to criminals when they combine it with data that already appears online. People-search websites and data brokers can contain your phone number, current or previous addresses and other identifying information. Scammers can combine those details with breached data to build a more complete profile of you. A personal data removal service can help reduce your online footprint by sending removal requests to data brokers on your behalf. Some services also continue checking to see whether your information reappears. No service can guarantee that every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Still, removing information from data broker databases can make it harder for scammers to gather additional details about you. You can make removal requests yourself as well. However, doing it manually can be time-consuming and may require repeated requests. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

If you discover that someone is using your information, act quickly. Visit the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website to report identity theft and create a personalized recovery plan. Keep records of suspicious transactions, emails and letters related to the fraud. Save copies of any reports you file as well. The sooner you spot suspicious activity, the sooner you can start limiting the damage.
Kurt's key takeaways

What bothers me most about the CareCloud breach is how little control you may have over where your medical information ends up. You can choose a doctor you trust. You can create strong passwords and protect your own devices. Yet some of your most sensitive information may still pass through another company's systems behind the scenes. That leaves millions of people dealing with the consequences when something goes wrong. If your information was involved, I would take the notification seriously even if everything looks normal today. A stolen Social Security number or medical record can remain useful to criminals long after the original breach fades from the news. Freeze your credit if your Social Security number was exposed. Watch your medical records and financial accounts over time. Then be especially cautious when an unexpected email, call or text seems to know surprisingly personal details about you. I would also reduce what data brokers can easily find about you and keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices. Those added layers can make follow-up attacks harder for scammers to pull off.
