title: Ratko Mladić, 'Butcher of Bosnia' convicted of genocide, dies at 84
summary: Ratko Mladić, the notorious Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide and war crimes, has died at age 84 in a Hague prison hospital while serving a life sentence.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb warlord general who oversaw wartime atrocities as he led forces that carried out the worst massacre in Europe since World War II, has died. He was 84.
Mladić, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia," died at a hospital in The Hague, Netherlands, U.N. court officials said.
He had been in custody since 2011 after years on the run for war crimes committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2017, he was sentenced to life in prison.
EX-PHILIPPINE PRESIDENT DUTERTE TO FACE TRIAL ON CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY CHARGES
Serb Gen. Ratko Mladić stands near a United Nations flag at Sarajevo Airport May 17, 1993. Mladić died Thursday. (AP Photo/Jerome Delay)
Mladić was one of the most notorious figures in the conflict that left more than 100,000 people dead and displaced more than a million others.

Under his command, Bosnian Serb troops took control of large swaths of Bosnia and Herzegovina and laid siege to the capital of Sarajevo and other cities. His forces detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers in concentration camps and systematically slaughtered prisoners.
Despite the charges levied against him, Mladić never showed remorse. In court, he yelled at the judges when he was sentenced.
Bosnian Serb Gen. Ratko Mladić speaks to soldiers near the Bosnian town of Cazin Sept. 4, 1994. (AP Photo/Radivoje Pavicic)

"He was murdered there, in those dungeons," Janko Seslija, a former Bosnian Serb soldier, told The Associated Press. "I feel sorry for Gen. Mladić. He was an honorable man, honorable soldier and commander."

A former Communist-era military officer, Mladić sided with the Serbs as Yugoslavia broke apart and disintegrated into war. He led a Serb insurgency in Croatia before taking over the Bosnian Serb army, according to The AP.
Among the horrors Mladić was charged with was the 1995 slaughter of up to 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica, which was supposed to be a safe zone guarded by Dutch peacekeepers.
A mural of former Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladić was vandalized with paint in Belgrade, Serbia, Sept. 20, 2022. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Mladić seized the town and assured the Muslim children that everything would be fine. Hours later, his troops began days of rape, torture and mass killings.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Experts zero in on likely cause of deadly Nepal mudslide, with more than 1,400 missing
summary: A massive glacier collapse triggered a magnitude 5.2 landslide event that caused catastrophic Nepal and Tibet floods, with over 1,400 people still missing.
story: Meteorologist Adam Klotz and geoscientist Simon Cook joined 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze the deadly glacial collapse, landslides and deadly floods along the China-Nepal border that left more than 1,300 missing.

The catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet now estimated to have killed hundreds were likely triggered by a massive glacier collapse and debris flow that registered as a magnitude 5.2 landslide, according to the U.S. Geological Service (USGS).

The USGS originally pinpointed the cause of the mudslides as a 4.4 magnitude earthquake but later updated its analysis after observing data from nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves and satellite imagery. That data suggested that no earthquake had occurred.
Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development told The Associated Press that Wednesday’s flash floods were likely triggered by a glacial avalanche.

"Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave," they said in a statement, adding that at one point, the water levels on the Trishuli River rose by as much as 27 feet in just a half hour.
TERRIFYING VIDEO CAPTURES PEOPLE FLEEING INCOMING MUDSLIDE AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER
Earthmovers clear the debris of flash flooding in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)
The death toll has climbed to more than 360 people estimated to have been killed in the floods along the Nepal-China border, the AP reported, citing local police.
Rescue teams are now searching for the more than 1,400 people who went missing during the chaos. Many of them were foreigners and pilgrims.
Nepal Police on Thursday began posting lists of Nepali and foreign nationals missing. Several dozen Americans were listed.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed to Fox News that as of 8 a.m. Thursday, there are approximately 90 Americans who may have been impacted by the floods. The U.S. embassies in Nepal and China are working to assist Americans in affected areas.

"The State Department is closely monitoring the situation and has deployed a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts," the spokesperson said. "The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities in Nepal."
The Nepalese army rescued more than 100 people from flood-hit areas by helicopter Thursday morning, according to army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet.
A vehicle is seen in the aftermath of flash floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district in Nepal on Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)
BABY PULLED FROM VEHICLE TRAPPED IN RAGING FLOODWATERS IN DRAMATIC RESCUE CAUGHT ON VIDEO
The flooding destroyed dozens of bridges and nearly 25 miles of roads, further complicating search and rescue efforts, according to Nepalese officials.

Bishal Kumar Bhandari, chairman of the Nepal Red Cross Society, told the AP that they have shifted focus to large-scale relief operations. He said that around 1,200 people were displaced from at least three villages.
Videos of the disaster showed raging floodwaters sweeping away cars, engulfing people trying to flee and destroying homes and bridges.
Debris was left tangled in tree branches and power lines, vehicles were buried and mud-covered survivors emerged as flooding cut off travel in some areas.

The village of Soley in Nuwakot, which has about 25 homes, was almost entirely destroyed, according to Kathmandu-based journalist Nirajan Paudyal, whose parents and other relatives live there. Desperate for news, he traveled to the area Thursday to check on his family.
"There is no update till now. I fear there won’t be any update," Paudyal told the AP.
A girl cries as she waits for news of relatives missing after flash floods in Bidur, Nepal's Nuwakot district, on Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)
11 VISITORS TRAPPED AS DANGEROUS FLASH FLOODING TEARS THROUGH ICONIC NATIONAL PARK
The Dalai Lama, the highest spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, released a message to those affected by the floods in the region.

"I am saddened to learn of the devastating floods in the Rasuwa region of Nepal and Kyirong in Tibet, resulting in loss of life and heavy structural damage," the 91-year-old leader said in a statement. "I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy."

He continued: "Since this region has seen calamities in the past as well, these are certainly symptoms of a deeper underlying cause — whether climate change or other factors. I hope that appropriate follow-up measures will be taken, wherever possible, to help ensure that such disasters do not recur."
People walk past damage in the aftermath of flash floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district in Nepal, on Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The disaster in Nepal and Tibet underscores a broader threat, as increasingly unstable Himalayan ice poses risks to communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions.

The region experienced similar flash flooding in August 2025, when high temperatures caused a glacial lake in Tibet to overflow. The resulting floods killed nine people and damaged critical infrastructure, including a bridge linking Nepal and China.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: US counters China as Beijing’s ‘shock wave’ hits African economies
summary: China's state-subsidized imports are crippling African manufacturing, a top State Department official says. The U.S. aims to offer alternatives and secure critical minerals supply.
story: China imposes retaliatory sanctions on U.S. firms and tightens drone export restrictions as trade tension escalates while Washington targets Chinese companies allegedly using Iranian fuel and weighs additional sanctions on Chinese A.I. firms.
JOHANNESBURG: A top State Department official has hit out at China for what analysts are calling "the China shock wave" effect now crippling African economies.

African manufacturing is reportedly being battered by a surge of Chinese imports. It’s a triple whammy — China takes raw materials, including critical minerals, from the continent and floods Africa with state-subsidized products. And Beijing isn’t importing anywhere near an equal amount of African products.
The China Global South Project reported that in 2025, Chinese exports to Africa hit $225 billion in value, whereas imports from Africa were roughly only half that — $123 billion.
PUTIN USING AFRICA AS ‘PURSE’ FOR UKRAINE WAR WHILE US FACES ‘INTELLIGENCE BLACK HOLE’: COMMANDER

China's Xi Jinping with President of the Comoros Azali Assoumani (L), South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Senegalese President Macky Sall attend the China-Africa Leaders' Roundtable Dialogue on the last day of the 2023 BRICS Summit in Johannesburg on Aug.24, 2023. (Alet Pretorius/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Now the Trump administration aims to change this imbalance — and create opportunities for American businesses.

"China continues to flood Africa with exports," Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia told Fox News Digital. He added, "No country is immune to the negative impacts of China’s unfair trade practices and state-subsidized overcapacity. China’s economic engagement with African countries has often led to unsustainable debt, economic coercion and an oversupply of Chinese imports threatening to displace and preventing the development of local industries."

He continued, "The U.S. government aims to offer credible alternatives that leverage public and private financing in priority areas that make America safer, stronger and more prosperous. The United States is committed to maintaining the strong, open investment environment that benefits our economy and our people, while enhancing our ability to protect our nation from new and evolving threats that can accompany foreign investment."

Elaine Dezenski, senior director and head of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital China is the number one trading partner for many African countries but warned "that doesn’t mean that African countries are moving up the value chain. On the contrary, some African countries are increasingly tied into a cycle of mineral and other natural resource exports to China, only to be on the receiving end of finished goods, also from China."
WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA
A general view of the Chinese-built Maputo-Katembe Bridge taken on Nov. 10, 2018 in Maputo, Mozambique. (Roberto Matchissa/AFP via Getty Images)

Dezenski added, "Africa wants to manufacture. Chinese exports are getting in the way. Key exports from China are substituting for specific products that could be manufactured in Africa. As China is increasingly shut out of U.S. and European markets through high tariff regimes, Africa is feeling the effects, while China still claims it's supporting emerging economies."

China has lent the money to build new roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Mozambique. But in this, the fifth-poorest country in the world where jobs are in short supply, Beijing insisted that Chinese companies should do the construction. Mozambicans in some cases stood by, while workers brought 7,000 miles from Beijing to dig up the streets became a feature in this African country.

Beijing has now targeted Africa in another way. Between 17% and 40% of all car sales in South Africa are for vehicles from China. The goal appears not to stop at imports. The Chinese government-owned carmaker Chery has recently bought South Africa’s Nissan plant, and will make Chinese models such as Jetour near Johannesburg.

Chery Automobile Chairman Yin Tongyue (R2) and South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile (R3) attend the launch of the Chery manufacturing facility at the former Nissan factory on July 3, 2026, in Rosslyn, Pretoria, South Africa. China's Chery formally took over Nissan's car manufacturing plant in Rosslyn on Friday under a deal that was announced in January, and executives said the company will spend millions of dollars upgrading and adding machinery ahead of starting vehicle production in South Africa in mid-2027. (Sun Xiang/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images)

But China has won over many South African consumers. "China is delivering better vehicles and better prices to South African consumers — and this is pushing Western-oriented firms out of the market," analyst Frans Cronje told Fox News Digital.

Cronje, president of the Washington-based Yorktown Foundation for Freedom, added, "The South African and broader sub-Saharan business communities have always shown a Western lean or bias, in large part a consequence of the region's colonial past. But China's industrial influence is changing, and as the South African vehicle industry shows, that change can be rapid and occur with the support of consumers. Privately, many Western firms say they don’t know if they can remain competitive."

The U.S. is making its own waves in Africa though. The administration’s Bureau of African Affairs has reported it has worked on 37 commercial transactions that have closed since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term — representing $25.67 billion in total value, with more still being reported.

A sign at the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA) memorial park in Lusaka, Zambia, on Thursday, Sept. 21, 2023. For over a decade, China poured more than $120 billion of government-backed loans through its Belt and Road Initiative to build hydropower plants, roads and rail lines across the continent as well as unparalleled influence. (Zinyange Auntony/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

There’s a way to go. While American goods traded with Africa last year were valued at $83.4 billion by the Office of the United States Trade Representative, Beijing’s General Administration of Customs claimed bilateral trade between China and Africa reached $348 billion for the same period.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The will to succeed, though, is clear. Assistant Secretary Garcia added, "The United States is committed to reshaping the global critical minerals and rare earths market to make it more diverse, secure and reliable. We will work with African partners to address risks from non-market actors and ensure supply chain security. We are using diplomatic and economic tools to promote fair and transparent markets that work for everyone."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Chinese Embassy spokesman in Washington, D.C., for comment.
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Dominican Republic joins global fight against antisemitism with landmark move
summary: Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun called the Dominican Republic's IHRA adoption a "historic moment" and urged other Latin American governments to follow suit.
story: The Department of Justice has launched an investigation into New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani following allegations of unequal treatment of Jewish residents. Fox News national correspondent CB Cotton details the growing concerns over antisemitism in New York City, highlighting a DOJ letter demanding answers.

The Dominican Republic is set to become the 48th country in the world and the seventh in Latin America to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism after President Luis Abinader ordered the country’s foreign ministry to formalize the decision.

The move came as Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, the U.S. special envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, urged other Latin American governments to follow the Dominican Republic’s lead, pointing to the Trump administration’s efforts at home as a framework for confronting antisemitism internationally.

Abinader made the announcement Monday at the Combat Antisemitism Movement-sponsored annual Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism in the nation's capital, Santo Domingo. According to an English translation of the president’s remarks, Abinader said antisemitism should not be viewed as a threat affecting only Jewish communities. "Antisemitism is not a problem that concerns only the Jewish people," he said. "It is a threat to democratic coexistence and to the rights and freedoms of us all."
A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT
Dominican Republic President Luis Abinader addresses CAM's sixth-annual Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism, in Santo Domingo, Aug. 25, 2026. (Combat Antisemitism Movement)

The announcement comes amid heightened concern over antisemitism worldwide. The Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center monitored and reported 767 antisemitic incidents globally in March 2026, an average of nearly 25 incidents per day and a 32.5% increase compared with March 2025.
Kaploun praised the Dominican Republic’s decision at the conference as a "historic moment" and called on other governments across the region to follow its lead.
"What you have witnessed tonight is a government standing up for what is right," he said.
"There cannot be any compromise with antisemitism," he continued. "We will lead by example, and we will take positive steps to protect every Jewish community."
Kaploun pointed to the Trump administration’s efforts in the United States as a framework other governments could use to confront antisemitism within their own institutions.
'NOT ON OUR WATCH': GLOBAL LAW ENFORCEMENT LEADERS UNITE IN POLAND AGAINST HATE

U.S. special envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, Rabbi Ambassador Yehuda Kaploun, speaks at a meeting of Latin American lawmakers during CAM's Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism, Aug. 25, 2026. (Combat Antisemitism Movement)

"In America, we have our marching orders," he said. "We are holding universities accountable. We are prosecuting hate crimes. We have changed our visa vetting programs. We have withdrawn from major U.N. bodies that have promoted terrorism and antisemitism."

The U.S. State Department has used a working definition of antisemitism, together with guiding examples, since 2010. In 2016, the IHRA’s member countries adopted the current non-legally binding working definition.

The IHRA describes antisemitism as "a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews." It further explains that antisemitism can include rhetorical or physical manifestations directed against Jewish or non-Jewish individuals, their property, Jewish community institutions or religious facilities.

Its non-legally binding definition and accompanying examples are intended to help governments, law enforcement agencies, universities and other institutions identify contemporary manifestations of antisemitism and respond to incidents more consistently.
CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM
Close-ups of antisemitic graffiti scrawled across Israeli-American Council headquarters in Los Angeles. (The Israeli-American Council (IAC) national headquarters in Los Angeles)

The accompanying examples address conduct including Holocaust denial, conspiracy theories about Jewish power, holding Jewish people collectively responsible for Israel’s actions and applying standards to Israel that are not demanded of other democratic nations.

As of the end of 2025, 1,334 governments, public institutions, universities, nonprofit organizations, corporations and sports organizations worldwide had adopted or endorsed the IHRA definition, according to data compiled by the Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center.
Anti-Israel protesters holding antisemitic posters in Alberta, Canada, on April 13, 2025. (Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via AP)

Abinader told the conference that, "Rejecting antisemitism does not mean taking a position regarding a particular government or conflict," he added. "It means stating unequivocally that no political disagreement, no cause and no circumstance can justify hatred, discrimination, or violence against an individual or a community."

Abinader said the definition would provide the country with a framework for identifying and combating different forms of antisemitism while respecting freedom of expression and other rights protected by the Dominican Constitution.
CRITICS SAY TURKEY'S VERBAL ATTACKS ON ISRAEL HAVE CROSSED INTO ANTISEMITISM

"Through this decision, the Dominican Republic reaffirms its commitment to the memory of the Holocaust, to the protection of Jewish communities and to the eradication of antisemitism in all its forms," he said. "Human dignity is indivisible and its defense admits no exceptions."

The president connected the decision to the Dominican Republic’s history of offering refuge to Jews fleeing Nazi persecution. Following the 1938 Évian Conference, hundreds of Jewish refugees established a community in Sosúa, where they were able to rebuild their lives.
Abinader also announced that his government would commit 50 million Dominican pesos toward constructing a new building for the Jewish Museum of Sosúa to preserve that history.

Lawmakers from 19 Latin American nations visit the Dominican Chamber of Deputies, in Santo Domingo, during CAM's Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism, Aug. 24, 2026. (Combat Antisemitism Movement)
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Once the Foreign Ministry formalizes the decision, the Dominican Republic will join Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Panama and Uruguay as the Latin American countries that have embraced the IHRA framework.
The decision adds to growing regional acceptance of the definition and could set a precedent for additional Latin American governments considering how to formally identify and address antisemitism.

Dominican Republic's President Luis Abinader (R) gestures as he speaks next to Vice President Raquel Pena during his annual report at the National Congress in Santo Domingo on Feb. 27, 2026. (Danny Polaco / AFP via Getty Images)

Abinader concluded his remarks with a call for the region to act: "From this land, which at different moments in its history has offered refuge and hope, let us send a firm message throughout Latin America and the Caribbean: Indifference must never prevail in the face of hatred."
"May this forum enable us to turn memory into education; education into prevention; and our principles into concrete action," he added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kaploun framed that regional effort as one the United States is prepared to support, saying he was representing President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in delivering a direct message to Latin American leaders: "America stands ready to support our friends in this effort to bring a new Latin America with religious liberty and freedom for everybody."

Ariella Noveck is a journalist specializing in antisemitism and Middle East affairs, with extensive experience covering Jewish communities worldwide. She can be followed on X and Instagram @AriellaNoveck

title: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch defeats a younger challenger in Massachusetts primary
summary: Lynch won against Patrick Roath, NBC News projects, who is more than three decades younger and came at him from the left.
story: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch has defeated a younger, more progressive primary challenger, NBC News projects, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents after a turbulent primary season.

Lynch, 71, won renomination over Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. With his win, Lynch staved off an attempt to add him to the list of Democratic officeholders dethroned by rivals pushing for generational change.
Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal also secured renomination, defeating teacher Jeromie Whalen in another Democratic primary.

On the other side of Massachusetts, Roath outraised Lynch, outspent him significantly on the airwaves and scored The Boston Globe editorial board’s endorsement to go with backing from Patrick, progressive activist David Hogg’s group, Leaders We Deserve, and key teachers unions.

That support helped Roath press Lynch for months in one of the toughest fights of his political career. He highlighted Lynch’s various breaks with his party in the past, including votes against the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, for the Laken Riley Act. Roath also called for progressive measures like “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE and restricting military aid to Israel.

But Lynch persevered, trumpeting work that he says held the Trump administration accountable and leaning on his decades of experience, including deep relationships with unions and other fixtures in the district.

“I got to know this district by living here and regularly attending hundreds of town meetings, not just to speak, but to listen and understand the needs and priorities of the people that I represent,” Lynch said at an August forum sponsored by the League of Women Voters Hingham and others.

He touted “tens of billions of dollars that I’ve been able to bring back to our district” and added that he “accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress. You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.”

Lynch’s victory means he has avoided the fate of 11 of his House colleagues — including seven Democrats — who lost primary challenges this year as voters took some of their frustrations with Washington out on incumbent lawmakers. Another two senators, both Republicans whose primary opponents got Trump endorsements, also lost primaries this year.

Neal also avoided defeat in another primary marked by arguments over generational change and progressive policy proposals. Whalen, 39, a high school teacher, ran a campaign decrying the “old-school political entanglements that got us into this mess” and called to abolish ICE and cut off U.S. military aid to Israel.
Neal spent more than $1 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, about 10 times what Whalen spent.
Meanwhile, in the open 6th District, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who ran for the Senate but lost that primary to Sen. Ed Markey.
Koh was an aide to a variety of top Democrats, including former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, and chief of staff of the U.S. Labor Department, and he was the top fundraiser in the race.

Both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris have appeared in an ad for Koh, who has emphasized that he wants to take on Trump and his “corruption,” calling to abolish ICE and pass “Medicare for All.”

title: Alaska finalizes Senate race for November: 3 Republicans — 2 Dans Sullivan — and 1 Democrat
summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola will be the only Democrat on the ballot after Democrat David Leslie, who finished fourth in the primary, withdrew.
story: The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election.
Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot.

The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns.

Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign.

The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary.
They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
Tom Begich, a Democrat who finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

title: Whistleblower says USPS system Trump ordered for mail ballots is flawed and untested
summary: An executive order from Trump, which is stymied in the courts, required the Postal Service to rapidly build a complex system to vet mail ballots.
story: An anonymous federal official warned in a whistleblower complaint this week that the technical system the U.S. Postal Service built for mail voting is flawed, untested and likely to cause major disruptions in this fall’s midterm elections if it is implemented.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March that directed his administration to create federal lists of citizens and asked the Postal Service to transmit mail ballots to only those people. A federal judge has blocked the order from going into effect amid ongoing litigation over its constitutionality; the whistleblower complaint highlights potential issues that could arise if the courts ultimately declare it lawful.

The USPS typically is responsible only for transporting mail ballots between election officials and voters, and the federal government has never kept a central list of all American citizens. Trump ordered the agency to take on an unprecedented and complex role in the process this year amid a broader attempt to exert greater control over the country’s elections and his continued unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

The technical system the USPS assembled to vet voters was developed in a “rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed process,” according to a whistleblower complaint sent to the office of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Blumenthal sent the complaint to Postmaster General David Steiner on Monday, asking for more information.

“This administration seems hell-bent on changing the framework of casting ballots in this country, clearly for political reasons,” Blumenthal said on a call with reporters Monday. “It is unconstitutional, as is argued in the courts by the litigation that is ongoing, but this disclosure indicates that it is also blatantly incompetent and incapable of actually delivering ballots that are lawful in this midterm election.”
In a statement Tuesday, the White House disputed the whistleblower’s allegations.

“The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail barcodes for a wide variety of large customers,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson.

The whistleblower is identified as an anonymous federal official who is being represented by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit group that represents public- and private-sector employees making such complaints. They allege that the USPS didn’t begin building its portal for verifying ballots “in earnest” until June, giving itself less than three months to complete a system that would ordinarily take at least nine to 12 months to build.

The agency last month finalized the rule for how it would implement the changes, which would create a massive new workload for election officials and put up hurdles for millions of voters to cast ballots by mail.
A spokesperson for the USPS said the agency had received Blumenthal’s letter and is “carefully reviewing the concerns he and the whistleblower have raised.”

“The United States Postal Service has spent months developing a U.S. Federal Ballot Mail Portal to provide election officials with a simple, secure, and efficient way to share lists of individuals receiving ballots by mail in their respective states,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The portal is just one part of a broader, year-round effort by the Postal Service to ensure that election mail and ballots are handled and delivered securely, reliably, and efficiently.”
Large batches of ballots would be rejected by the portal if even a single ballot couldn’t be verified, the whistleblower said.

“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state — effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the complaint reads. “Even under ordinary circumstances this would be problematic because of predictable errors in any barcode scanning process.”

The whistleblower said workers involved in developing the USPS system feared it would crash and described the process just days before the project was originally scheduled to be released to the public Tuesday as a “s--- show,” according to the complaint.
The whistleblower also said the USPS had ordered workers to continue developing its system, despite court orders blocking implementation of the project.
A federal court order Monday said the government could continue building its portal as long as the states aren’t required to participate.

title: No plans for ICE to be at polls for midterms, DHS says
summary: A senior DHS official said ICE will do its regular duties on the day of midterm elections, though Secretary Markwayne Mullin said agents would enter a polling place to serve a warrant.
story: ICE officers have not received guidance telling them they need to do anything in addition to their regular duties on the day of November’s midterm elections, a senior Homeland Security official told NBC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a news conference Tuesday in New York that ICE officers will be at a polling place only if “there is a threat to that polling place” or if officers are serving a warrant on someone “that we have been actively tracking down.”
“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” Mullin said.
Asked whether ICE officers would enter polling places, Mullin said they would if they had warrants.
“If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be,” Mullin said.

President Donald Trump and Mullin have claimed without offering any evidence that there are over 250,000 noncitizens on voter rolls across several states. Mullin recently threatened state election officials with possible prison time if they didn’t comply with the administration’s methods to determine whether noncitizens were on their voter rolls. Several state officials have pushed back against sharing private state voter roll data that includes personal information, such as Social Security numbers.

title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
summary: Officials in Tarrant County, the third most-populous in Texas, approved a plan to reduce the number of polling locations by 92 compared to the 2022 elections.
story: Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates.

Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites.
The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it.

Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington.
Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote.
The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican.
Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote.
“The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose.
Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years.

Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years.

“The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.”
Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.”
Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area.
“There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said.
A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources.

“I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

title: Judge rules that the trial of Tyler Robinson in Charlie Kirk’s killing can go forward
summary: A judge in Utah is expected to decide whether there is enough evidence to move forward with a trial against the man accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk.
story: A judge in Utah on Tuesday ruled that a trial for the 23-year-old man accused of fatally shooting prominent conservative political activist Charlie Kirk can move forward.

District Judge Tony Graf issued the decision after a day of arguments in a probable cause hearing. Prosecutors argued there was enough evidence against Tyler Robinson to proceed with the case, while defense attorneys maintained that the evidence was insufficient.
“It is hereby ordered that the defendant, Tyler James Robinson, is bound over for trial,” Graf said.
Robinson’s defense attorney then entered pleas of not guilty on all counts on his behalf. The next court date was set for Oct. 23.
Prosecutors have charged Robinson with aggravated murder, a first-degree felony that makes him eligible for the death penalty, and other counts.

Robinson is accused of killing Kirk with a single rifle round fired from a rooftop at an event at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10. The assassination of Kirk, the 31-year-old co-founder of the youth advocacy group Turning Point USA and a close ally of President Donald Trump, rocked U.S. politics.
In the lead-up to his ruling, Graf allowed lawyers on both sides to present closing arguments Tuesday. Evidence was presented in July.

“It’s not difficult to understand the motive here,” Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court during the state’s closing arguments. “The defendant’s views were repugnant to the positions that Charlie Kirk famously took.”
McBride alleged that Robinson threatened the lives of the people who attended Kirk’s event last September.
“You can’t shoot a rifle into a crowd of 3,000 people without knowing that you create a great risk of death to all those around your target,” McBride said in part.
Robinson’s defense attorney, Richard Novak, said the state can’t prove what would have motivated the shooting.
“There’s no evidence as to really what was in Mr. Robinson’s mind, if in fact he was the shooter, about Charlie Kirk,” Novak said.
“Because we have no testimony that Mr. Robinson had ever spoken about Charlie Kirk, that he’d ever heard anything he’d said, that he’d ever discussed anything” about Kirk in the past, Novak said.
Another defense attorney, Staci Visser, argued that Utah’s legal aggravator that Robinson’s act posed a great risk of death to others does not apply because multiple shots or threats were not made.
“There is one act, there is one shot, there is one bullet, there is one victim,” she said.
Graf in his ruling allowed the aggravator and said the state met its burden at this preliminary stage, but he did not rule on the merits.

Tuesday’s high-stakes hearing came nearly two months after prosecutors laid out a detailed public reconstruction of the alleged events surrounding Kirk’s killing and presented a trove of evidence against Robinson, including security video, digital records and forensic material.

David Hull, a former State Bureau of Investigation agent, characterized Robinson’s alleged movements before and after the assassination. Hull’s testimony at a five-day hearing was accompanied by excerpts from campus video shown in court for the first time.

Robinson arrived at the university hours before the shooting, bought a meal from a campus Chick-fil-A restaurant and made contact with representatives for Turning Point USA, Hull testified. Robinson then changed outfits and took a position on a rooftop overlooking the amphitheater where Kirk was speaking, Hull said.

In a video shown in court July 7, Robinson could be seen crouching on the rooftop, Hull told the court. Then, after a bullet hit Kirk, Robinson could be seen darting across the roof, dropping to ground level and sprinting away on foot, Hull added.
Prosecutors played another video featuring partially redacted excerpts from law enforcement investigators’ interview with Lance Twiggs, Robinson’s former romantic partner and roommate.

The day after Kirk’s assassination, Twiggs told investigators, Robinson nervously paced their apartment and expressed regret. Twiggs told investigators that he asked Robinson whether it was true that he fatally shot Kirk.
In the emotional interaction that followed, according to Twiggs, Robinson “said he wishes he hadn’t done it.”
Twiggs told investigators that Robinson said he intended to confess to his parents or go to the police. He turned himself in to law enforcement authorities later that day.

Investigators have said they found the suspected murder weapon — a bolt-action rifle — wrapped in a towel in a wooded area near the Utah Valley University amphitheater. DNA from both Robinson and Twiggs was on the towel, Sgt. Jennifer Faumuina of the Utah Department of Public Safety testified July 7.
Robinson’s lawyers tried to throw doubt on the DNA evidence and pressed a defense witness, FBI forensic analyst Amanda Bakker, about the potential for error in forensic testing and other issues.
Robinson’s defense lawyers have not provided an alternative theory for who killed Kirk.

In a charging document filed last September, prosecutors highlighted inscriptions alleged to have been etched on each round of the rifle, including the phrases “Hey Fascist! Catch!” and “If you Read This, You are GAY.”

Twiggs, in the recorded interview played in court, told investigators that Robinson never talked about Kirk before the shooting. The roommates-turned-partners had originally bonded over their shared love of video games, Twiggs said.
Kirk family attorney Jeffrey Neiman on Tuesday asked that the court act swiftly and to “set this trial as soon as practically possible.”
“The United States Constitution guarantees criminal defendants many rights. The right to delay is not among them,” Neiman said.

title: Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting.
summary: Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, Colin Kaepernick is back in the spotlight.
story: Colin Kaepernick still puts in a workout at 4:30 a.m. most days. His football life may be long over, but his life’s work is not.
Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, the former star quarterback is stepping back into the spotlight.
Add to Google
Add to Google

His memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” comes out on Sept. 15. And in interviews with NBC News, his first time speaking in depth about his protest’s fallout in years, Kaepernick reveals the story behind how he came to take a knee in 2016, an act that made him both a hero and a pariah, and one of the most divisive figures in the country.

Kaepernick, 38, is now also a father of a 4-year-old girl. That, he says, helped him understand he has unfinished business in his life and cause. Being a dad “increases the responsibility and urgency of the work we’re doing,” he says. He doesn’t want his daughter — or anyone else — to think he stopped fighting or that the fight was not worth it.  “I don’t want my community to watch me and have the takeaway be that if you fight for Black folks, it’s over for you,” he writes in his book.
More NBC News coverage of Colin Kaepernick

Kaepernick will be the first guest on "Before & After with Lester Holt," available as soon as Sept. 7.Kaepernick is set to appear on "TODAY" on Sept. 16.Read Kaepernick's response to Jay-Z's recent freestyle rap about him on NBC News on Wednesday.
Kaepernick will be the first guest on "Before & After with Lester Holt," available as soon as Sept. 7.
Kaepernick is set to appear on "TODAY" on Sept. 16.
Read Kaepernick's response to Jay-Z's recent freestyle rap about him on NBC News on Wednesday.

Much has shifted in American politics, culture, sports and policing since 2016. And much work still needs to be done, Kaepernick says, which is why he chose now to recount the decade-long odyssey that began with a quiet protest during the national anthem.

Though the years have provided perspective, Kaepernick says they haven’t dulled his displeasure with the NFL. The quarterback who once led the San Francisco 49ers on a Disney movie-esque run to the Super Bowl in 2012 says he hasn’t watched an NFL game since he was exiled from the league.

“I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well,” Kaepernick says. “I watch college football.”
(NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has said on multiple occasions he doesn’t believe Kaepernick was blackballed.)

On Sept. 1, 2016, Kaepernick and his San Francisco 49ers teammate Eric Reid kneeled during the national anthem before a preseason game. It was not the first time Kaepernick didn’t stand. His protest actually began a month earlier, on Aug. 14, when he sat on the bench during “The Star-Spangled Banner.”
The idea had simmered in the months prior to the season when, he writes in his memoir, he was recuperating from surgeries. He might not have taken a knee if he hadn’t injured it first.

The rehab gave him more free time than he ever had in his life. And in the midst of news of police violence, Kaepernick immersed himself in literature on Black liberation, reading books such as “The Autobiography of Malcolm X” and “Black Skin, White Masks” by Frantz Fanon.

title: Customers are losing their appetites over disturbing AI-generated menus
summary: AI “slop” is increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.
story: AI “slop” is now increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.

As AI image-making technology has grown more advanced — and cheaper to use, in some cases being free — images with a distinct “slop” flavor, namely ones with surreal or even disturbing attributes, have begun appearing on bodega, café and restaurant menus.
There’s the shrimp scampi whose shrimp look more like miniature life preservers.
A breakfast burrito with filling that looks more like something out of a horror movie.
And “protein” options that look like they’re covered in bugs.
One X user said she attempted to order an item advertised on a café’s outdoor menu only to learn it didn’t exist and was instead the product of ChatGPT.

The trend comes as the use of AI has grown from a tech-employee specialty to a nearly ubiquitous pursuit among white-collar workers — and as overall inflation in the economy has remained stubborn. The confluence of lingering cost pressures and advancing technology appears to be translating into a boom in smaller businesses deploying AI-designed graphics and logos.

There have been real-world consequences to the trend of AI slop making the jump from online into the real world. A coffee shop in San Francisco paid hundreds of dollars to have graffiti removed that appeared to be in response to its use of AI-generated food images on its facade, SFGate reported.

“I want people to come to our restaurant, but, like, why is this such a big deal that it influences people on such intense level?” co-owner Lyndsey Lozano told the outlet. “Like, is it really that horrific that you have to act on such a feeling?”
Lozano could not be reached for additional comment.

Many of the establishments displaying the food images likely created by AI are smaller, likely family-owned establishments, said Paul Shovlin, an assistant professor of English at Ohio University who studies AI. He said that it may simply be the case that many of the places displaying the AI food are running on shoestring budgets.
For some longtime designers, the advent of AI-related image making has been maddening — not to mention bad for their bottom lines.

title: Student who felt ‘humiliated’ by ICE ankle monitor dies by suicide
summary: Pierre Damas Bel, 20, expressed feeling “shame and humiliation” at having to wear by an ankle monitor. The college student died by suicide days later.
story: Hours before Ohio college student and athlete Pierre Damas Bel took his own life Monday morning, he called his father for help.

It was around 8 a.m., and he was sitting inside his car on the side of Interstate 70, struggling mentally and emotionally with the shame of being forced to wear an ankle monitor by immigration officials. Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian student at Wright State University, said he had been bullied at school and felt “humiliated” by the device.
“I told him to come home so we can talk,” Bel’s father said in an emailed statement. “Around 11 the police showed at my door to report that my son threw himself under a truck.”
Bel stepped into oncoming traffic and died from his injuries, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said. His family blamed the humiliation brought on by the ankle monitor he had been wearing since July.
Carl Ruby, a local pastor and immigration advocate, said in a statement that Bel’s family wanted people to know it was a suicide related to immigration policies.

Bel arrived in the U.S. in 2024 and applied for admission into the country using the now-defunct CBP One app, Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in an emailed statement. He was released into the country and settled in Springfield with his parents and two brothers.

Bel excelled in academics and athletics, becoming an honor roll student at Springfield High School and joining JROTC. He was recruited to play soccer at Wittenberg University and hoped to attend medical school after college, immigration advocates said.

In May, the Springfield City School District featured Bel in a Facebook post highlighting recipients of a local scholarship that offered $2,500 to each student. Bel wore a blue suit and a black bow tie as he accepted his award, with a big smile on his face.
The future seemed bright.
Things began to change July 29, when ICE placed him in an “alternatives to detention program” with an ankle monitor while he continued his immigration proceedings.
He documented the experience on social media, writing July 30 that he came to the country to study, not “commit a crime or hurt anyone.”
“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote.

Bel was one of the roughly 300,000 Haitian nationals living in the U.S. who lost their temporary protected status, or TPS, at the end of July following a Supreme Court decision. The policy change triggered a wave of fear and confusion in Springfield, where 12,000 Haitians live.
ICE said it does not comment on the cause of death while an investigation is pending.
“We will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals,” it said in an emailed statement.

According to the Wittenberg University men’s soccer team, Bel was no longer able to play for the team after he lost TPS. He transferred to nearby Wright State University and immediately faced taunts and bullying from students, his family said.
“We do not want to politicize this, but this is a political problem, and the only solution is a political solution,” Ruby told reporters Tuesday.
“The only way that this will never be correct is if Republican elected officials join us in demanding better policy,” he said.
Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, has criticized the Trump administration’s harsh immigration enforcement and its impact on Ohio residents.
On Tuesday, he called Bel’s suicide a “horrible tragedy” that never should have happened.
“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name?” he told reporters.
Springfield, a small city in southwestern Ohio, became the center of salacious and unfounded rumors about the Haitian community during the 2024 presidential election.

In August, ICE began alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they were given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until immigration judges can decide whether they may have legitimate reasons to remain in the country, such as asylum claims.

Ankle monitors are usually issued because of a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost TPS after the Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official has said.

Some Springfield residents saw the arrival of Haitian nationals as a driving force behind the city’s economic renaissance. Others complained that Springfield was not prepared to welcome so many immigrants, who contributed to long waits at clinics and were driving up rental prices. Despite the unwanted attention, many Haitian residents thrived in their adopted home, taking jobs in manufacturing, buying homes and opening businesses.
Occasionally tensions boiled over. White supremacist groups and alt-right influencers have clashed with local immigration advocates and faith leaders who sought to protect the Haitian community.

Viles Dorsainvil, co-founder and executive director of the Haitian Support Center, said the Bel family is one of several hundred who have poured into the center seeking legal help and guidance. He estimates 34 people have been detained since TPS ended.
Bel’s is believed to be the first suicide in Springfield related to immigration enforcement, he said.
“I know many folks are depressed right now,” Dorsainvil said. “I never had in my mind that it would have gotten to that point.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

story: Richard Engel is back in Ukraine to report on its intensifying war with Russia, with a strike this weekend on a warehouse west of Kyiv becoming its deadliest attack this year — more than 38 people were killed.

title: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after extended Iran deployment
summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.
story: LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.

The toll of the more than nine-month deployment, most of it spent supporting military operations in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, was visible on the carrier as it pulled into Laem Chabang Port in Chonburi province. Paint has worn off and the metal underneath is rusted on the 1,092-foot warship, which is one of the largest in the world.

The Lincoln is stopping in Thailand on its journey home after having spent weeks in the headlines as the lengthy deployment raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.

The U.S. Navy confirmed the ship’s arrival in a statement, saying the Lincoln strike group arrived in Laem Chabang while the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sriracha and the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls went to Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.
The Navy said it was the Lincoln’s first full port stop after 286 days at sea since the deployment began in November.
Thai police crackdown on sex workers

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” said Rear Adm. Robert E. Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3. “It also underscores the strong and enduring partnership and alliance between the United States and Thailand.”
Service members could be seen working aboard the deck of the Lincoln as loudspeakers played announcements about the process for disembarkation, which is expected later in the day.
Lincoln will be at Laem Chabang port for four days, according to a U.S. military official. Each service member will get three “liberty days” and one day of duty aboard the ship.

About 5,000 sailors and Marines, some of them on two accompanying naval vessels, are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya, a nearby coastal resort city, for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop before they return to their home port, San Diego.

Locals in tourism-dependent Pattaya have eagerly awaited the arrival of the Lincoln, which pulled into sight from the shore after sunrise before it made a wide turn and harbored itself at a major cargo terminal.

Officials in Pattaya, where international tourist arrivals have dropped because of travel disruptions and soaring fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, say the visit is expected to inject about $3 million into the local economy.
Authorities have stepped up security, with heightened police patrols and checks along the roads. Businesses here are also trying to woo the sailors, with some putting up banners to welcome them.
Wichai Yuankham, 35, a factory worker who came to watch the ships arrive, said the naval visit was a welcome boost to the local economy.
“I am just excited to see the destroyer docking,” he said. “This is my first time seeing the destroyer, and I feel good seeing it, and we can boast to our neighboring countries about this.”

title: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch defeats a younger challenger in Massachusetts primary
summary: Lynch won against Patrick Roath, NBC News projects, who is more than three decades younger and came at him from the left.
story: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch has defeated a younger, more progressive primary challenger, NBC News projects, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents after a turbulent primary season.

Lynch, 71, won renomination over Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. With his win, Lynch staved off an attempt to add him to the list of Democratic officeholders dethroned by rivals pushing for generational change.
Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal also secured renomination, defeating teacher Jeromie Whalen in another Democratic primary.

On the other side of Massachusetts, Roath outraised Lynch, outspent him significantly on the airwaves and scored The Boston Globe editorial board’s endorsement to go with backing from Patrick, progressive activist David Hogg’s group, Leaders We Deserve, and key teachers unions.

That support helped Roath press Lynch for months in one of the toughest fights of his political career. He highlighted Lynch’s various breaks with his party in the past, including votes against the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, for the Laken Riley Act. Roath also called for progressive measures like “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE and restricting military aid to Israel.

But Lynch persevered, trumpeting work that he says held the Trump administration accountable and leaning on his decades of experience, including deep relationships with unions and other fixtures in the district.

“I got to know this district by living here and regularly attending hundreds of town meetings, not just to speak, but to listen and understand the needs and priorities of the people that I represent,” Lynch said at an August forum sponsored by the League of Women Voters Hingham and others.

He touted “tens of billions of dollars that I’ve been able to bring back to our district” and added that he “accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress. You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.”

Lynch’s victory means he has avoided the fate of 11 of his House colleagues — including seven Democrats — who lost primary challenges this year as voters took some of their frustrations with Washington out on incumbent lawmakers. Another two senators, both Republicans whose primary opponents got Trump endorsements, also lost primaries this year.

Neal also avoided defeat in another primary marked by arguments over generational change and progressive policy proposals. Whalen, 39, a high school teacher, ran a campaign decrying the “old-school political entanglements that got us into this mess” and called to abolish ICE and cut off U.S. military aid to Israel.
Neal spent more than $1 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, about 10 times what Whalen spent.
Meanwhile, in the open 6th District, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who ran for the Senate but lost that primary to Sen. Ed Markey.
Koh was an aide to a variety of top Democrats, including former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, and chief of staff of the U.S. Labor Department, and he was the top fundraiser in the race.

Both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris have appeared in an ad for Koh, who has emphasized that he wants to take on Trump and his “corruption,” calling to abolish ICE and pass “Medicare for All.”

title: GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent opponent clash in fiery Nebraska Senate debate
summary: Ricketts derided Osborn as a Democrat in all but name. Osborn said Ricketts isn’t representing Nebraska as they compete in a race on the fringe of the Senate battlefield.
story: Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., went on offense against independent opponent Dan Osborn in a debate Tuesday night, repeatedly calling him “Democrat Dan” throughout their meeting and associating his campaign with democratic socialists.

The debate will be the first of many across the country over the next two months as Democrats and Republicans battle for control of the Senate. Deep-red Nebraska is not usually home to nationally watched campaigns, but Osborn’s one-on-one contest with Ricketts could be closer than typical partisan contests in the state.
This debate, which took place at the Nebraska State Fair, may be the only clash between the two candidates with nine weeks to go until Election Day.
Osborn spent most of the debate distancing himself from both parties, but he was also careful not to completely cut ties with either side.

The Democratic nominee in the Senate race, Cindy Burbank, dropped out this summer, and the state Democratic Party chair said she was supporting Osborn. Osborn ran in 2024 and lost to GOP Sen. Deb Fischer by less than 7 percentage points even as Donald Trump carried the state by 20 points.

“I don’t need to caucus with either party,” Osborn said. “Nobody’s got a monopoly on a good idea. I will work with Republicans to get things passed, but it’s about delivering for Nebraska. That’s what I intend to do, is to work for the people of Nebraska, not a party boss.”

Ricketts drew stark differences between himself and his opponent, attacking Osborn over his support for “Medicare for All” and saying Osborn would not have supported the tax cuts and other measures in Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”

“Yes, I would have voted against the state that the current Big Beautiful Bill Act is in,” Osborn said. “But since we’re delving in hypotheticals, that act was passed by a tiebreaker for JD Vance. So if I would have beaten Deb Fischer and operated as a true independent in Washington, D.C., that would have been leverage. That would have been leverage to deliver for Nebraska.”

One of the major themes throughout the debate was PAC spending in both campaigns, as well as “dark money” coming from unidentified donors. Ricketts called out his opponent several times about his campaign finances, saying that his top fundraising sources were Washington, D.C., New York and California and that he’d gotten funds from top Democrats like Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

“Democrat Dan keeps trying to insinuate that somehow I can be part of this billionaires club or whatever,” Ricketts said. “The truth is I can’t be bought. He already has. He’s been paid for by those liberal out-of-state interests who are funding his campaign.”

After having mentioned several times throughout the debate that “dark money” is a problem in the election system that needs a fix, Osborn admitted that he has benefited from secret donors who have given to outside groups supporting his campaign.

“I don’t know who these people are, and they raise money in my name, and those are the ones that run ads,” Osborn said. “If it doesn’t say ‘I’m Dan Osborn’ or ‘I’m Pete Ricketts, I approve this message,’ that’s dark money working.”
The debate was broken into three parts, each individually focusing on tariffs and the cost of living, ICE and the war in Iran, and campaign financing and artificial intelligence.

title: Bill Simmons under review by Massachusetts authorities after admitting to proxy sports betting
summary: Simmons, the founder of The Ringer, said Tuesday that it was a “lesson learned” after FanDuel voided his wagers.
story: Bill Simmons, the popular sports podcaster who has championed sports betting, is under review by the Massachusetts Gaming Commission after he admitted on a recent episode to using his daughter’s boyfriend to place bets for him.

The commission announced the review Tuesday, two days after Simmons said on an episode of his podcast that he’d used a proxy on multiple occasions to log in to his account and make wagers in Massachusetts.
Simmons, founder of The Ringer, is based in California, where sports betting is not legal. In Massachusetts, mobile and online betting is allowed.
But proxy betting — having someone place bets on behalf of someone else — is illegal in Massachusetts and is not allowed by FanDuel, the sportsbook with which the wagers were issued.
“The Commission is aware of the comments made on the Bill Simmons Podcast and staff are currently reviewing the matter,” an MGC spokesman said in a statement.
FanDuel is the exclusive sports betting partner of The Ringer. A spokesperson for the sportsbook told NBC News it reported the matter to the MGC and voided Simmons’ bets.

On the podcast episode, Simmons said there were bets “that I really wanted to get in — the UCLA overs. But Houston, the market had not shifted appropriately yet. I can’t have my daughter do it; my dad would have no idea how to do it.”
But, Simmons said, he trusted his daughter’s boyfriend and allowed him to log in to his FanDuel account.

“I get the code to make sure it’s me to my phone, I give him the code, he logs in. And I have all this money that I had from last year because I actually hit a bunch of futures last year. And he’s putting in bets for me,” Simmons said, adding that “it was a real bonding moment for us.”
“A week later, I called him up, ran it back,” Simmons continued. “We did some more.”
In a new episode released Tuesday, Simmons said he was unaware that such bets could not be made.

“I talked about how I got my daughter’s boyfriend to place some bets for me in Massachusetts because I was in L.A. [I] did not know about the proxy rules,” he said. “Yeah, there are some real rules with this stuff, and they’ve ruled that not only are the bets going to be voided — and I learned my lesson.”
Simmons said he thought proxy betting was allowed. “There you go, lesson learned,” he said.

Simmons, a former ESPN columnist and commentator, is one of the most popular podcasters in the country. “The Bill Simmons Podcast,” as of Tuesday, ranked No. 22 overall and No. 2 in the sports category on Spotify.
Spotify acquired The Ringer — a sports and pop culture website and podcast network — in 2020 for more than $200 million, according to reports.

title: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey easily fends off Massachusetts primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton
summary: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Senate primary in Massachusetts, NBC News projects, in a victory for the party’s progressive wing.
story: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Senate primary in Massachusetts, NBC News projects, in a victory for the party’s progressive wing.
Markey was winning about two-thirds of the vote percentage points with 69% of the expected vote reporting.
See live results here

Markey’s win comes as other longtime Democratic lawmakers have lost to younger challengers in primaries this year. But the 80-year-old senator fended off his challenger by touting his liberal record as an author of the Green New Deal and vocal supporter of “Medicare for All.”

“It’s all about not just sending a Democrat to the Senate — it’s sending a progressive Democrat to the Senate from Massachusetts so there can be someone that reflects your values every single day,” Markey said at a rally on the eve of the primary, describing the race as “a progressive final round.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

Moulton said Tuesday night that he had called Markey “to congratulate him on his victory tonight.” Moulton told supporters that Markey “has my full support as our Democratic nominee, and we must stand united this November to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump.”

Moulton and his allies had a spending advantage in the race, spending $7.1 million on ads to Markey and his allies’ $3.9 million, according to AdImpact. That makes Markey’s win another victory for a progressive who faced an onslaught of well-funded attacks.

On the campaign trail and the airwaves, Markey also touted endorsements from progressive leaders, including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who both appeared in an ad for the senator, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Moulton, the 47-year-old congressman, called in his campaign for generational change — a call that has cost a handful of House Democrats their seats in primaries across the country this year. Markey was first elected to the Senate in 2013 after serving nearly 40 years in the House.

“Sen. Markey and I want the same things, but wanting isn’t winning, and the old way isn’t working,” Moulton said in one of his TV ads, listing policies including “tax the oligarchs, abolish ICE, pass healthcare for all.”

But Markey and his allies attacked Moulton for his past criticism of liberal policies. Commonwealth Together PAC, an outside group that has attacked Moulton, launched an ad saying the congressman opposes Medicare for All and taxing billionaires, pointing to 2019 comments from Moulton’s unsuccessful campaign for president.

Markey also sharply criticized Moulton on transgender issues, saying at the election-eve rally that Moulton “threw trans kids under the bus” after the 2024 election. Moulton told The New York Times after Democrats lost the presidential race: “I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Moulton apologized to “anyone hurt by those comments” in a recent debate.
In his primary campaign, Markey also vowed to continue fighting President Donald Trump.

“It’s a moment in history where Trump is challenging everything that started right here 250 years ago,” Markey said in one ad, referring to the country’s founding. “We have a message from Massachusetts: We are going to fight.”

title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
summary: Officials in Tarrant County, the third most-populous in Texas, approved a plan to reduce the number of polling locations by 92 compared to the 2022 elections.
story: Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates.

Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites.
The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it.

Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington.
Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote.
The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican.
Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote.
“The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose.
Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years.

Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years.

“The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.”
Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.”
Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area.
“There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said.
A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources.

“I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.
